title: The Inquisitor Prime — The Iron Hand of Purity
subtitle: Purity & Domination

lore.description:
Among the Aeler Iron Avengers, zealots, and witch-hunters, the Inquisitor Prime is venerated as the hand of absolute purity and the sword of uncompromising order. Where others see nuance, the Inquisitor sees corruption; where others see difference, they see contamination. Those who march beneath their sigil believe that no society can stand if it tolerates the impure or the disobedient. They hunt the arcane and the aberrant, not merely to destroy them, but to bind them as slaves to order—believing even the tainted may yet serve, so long as they are shackled.

**The office changes at the border.**

An Everflame Flame-Warden and a Temple Chain-Lantern can recognize the same invocation and deny that the other has any right to use it. The Warden serves a state faith whose purification is a published process. The Chain-Lantern speaks of investigation and rehabilitation under a faith that denies any priest stands between a soul and the light. Both can offer genuine protection from a danger. Both can keep a frightened person confined while sincerely calling the confinement necessary.

Their split inherited buildings, training, and families from the older church. A border house may still possess a censer made before the Synod of Thepyrgos separated in 478 AR. Its keeper can know the institution changed without believing the Patron departed. The hard question is which instructions the keeper followed afterward.

**The Accuser must also make a case.**

In the Covenant, the Inquisitor Prime is the Accuser. The office investigates and prosecutes; it does not make the investigator executioner by definition. Its scales and testimony stand within a faith founded on a dispossessed Sidhi woman's successful claim. An accusation has a respondent who must be heard.

Circuit work gave the office authority in places where local power preferred not to receive a complaint. Permanent houses later became vulnerable to their own patrons and routines. A prosecutor can uncover an actual abuse and then suppress the evidence that a benefactor profited by it. Another can refuse to prosecute a person whom an armed ally has already declared guilty. Neither difference requires a new Patron or a revised spell list.

**Watchers and Brine-Wardens.**

Pereshi Watchers Against the Maw invoke the Inquisitor with the Pale Shepherd against the unclean dead. Their ordinary work includes identifying remains and telling households what may be safely tended. Their quarrel with the Ash-Readers concerns whether a consuming hunger can be managed by feeding it sparingly. The Watchers fear that practice for reasons beyond dislike of dissent; their certainty has also carried fire into houses whose inhabitants needed help.

Zakov's Salt-Fire calls its protective order the Brine-Wardens. They drown people they sentence and call this a gentler purification. Households seeking help can fear that remedy as much as the danger reported to the order. Cooperation between the traditions grew through exchanged accounts of hauntings and stranded travelers. A Watcher arriving to help may be competent and still mistake a familiar funerary practice for evidence of corruption.

**Purity inside the hold.**

Aeler adherents can treat an unsafe opening or a neglected ward as a shared danger without treating all foreign neighbors as contamination. Which threat a hold has survived matters. A Himadri keeper's severe precautions and an Akazun keeper's readiness to replace damaged work can both serve protection. The difference cannot be reduced to one being devout and the other lax.

Set a conflict around an inspection that found something real. The proposed remedy would also destroy evidence, displace a household, or prevent another danger being repaired. Give the investigator grounds for urgency and someone able to challenge the remedy without denying the finding. The Patron's attraction is the promise that corruption can be recognized and opposed. Its human institutions become most dangerous when they decide that recognizing a danger makes every chosen response pure.
lore.followers: The Inquisitor Prime appears in vision as a faceless figure clad in burnished iron, with eyes like furnace-doors and a voice like grinding chains. To serve them is to embrace judgment without mercy and to live in suspicion of all who walk outside the prescribed law. For the faithful, doubt is treason; compassion is weakness; and freedom is the seed of ruin. In the wake of their followers, only silence and ash remain.

names_across_regions.ecktoria: The Unquenchable Fire of the Everflame, whose censers never cool
names_across_regions.aeler: The Light of Forges, whose hearths are kindled with a brand from the temple's eternal flame
names_across_regions.vhasia: The Gilded Judge, invoked by templars who swear to root out heretical magic

lore.quote: Mercy is weakness. Purity is survival. Where corruption hides, we carve it out.

domain_focus: Purity and Order: eradicating corruption, enforcing sacred law
Judgment: condemning the guilty, burning the heretical
Protection from the Tainted: warding against the supernatural
Domination: binding the impure to serve the pure

thiasos.description: The Inquisitor Prime's Thiasos is a small creature of zealous loyalty and keen perception: a white hound with brass eyes that can smell lies and taint, a ferret that hunts rodents of corruption with relentless efficiency, a bronze-feathered hawk that circles above suspected heretics, or a small mechanical bird that sings hymns of purity at dawn.
thiasos.care: Beyond its ordinary care, this Thiasos must be present at a daily prayer or rite of purification. If that need goes unmet, the Thiasos becomes Compromised: it growls at strangers or sings discordantly, imposing –1 die on all social rolls with those suspected of impurity for its bearer.

codex.description: A Codex sworn to the Inquisitor Prime is never a book of common knowledge. It may be an iron-bound ledger with pages of sanctified vellum, each Rite sealed with a drop of wax; a slate tablet that records only the names of the damned; or a scroll of censure that burns heretical text upon reading.
codex.upkeep: Because the Prime's laws are absolute, the Codex requires upkeep: the Runekeeper must spend an hour each week reciting each Rite aloud in a purified space, or the seals weaken (treat as Compromised until re-consecrated).

patrons_gift.name: The Iron Hand
patrons_gift.description: Once per scene as an action, a Runekeeper of the Inquisitor Prime may touch a held item (weapon, shield, or badge of office) and speak a word of judgment.
patrons_gift.effect: For the rest of the scene, the item grants +1 die to Investigation or Command rolls when confronting supernatural creatures, and the first time each scene the bearer would be affected by a magical illusion or fear effect, they may reroll the resistance check (the Prime's light burns through deception).
patrons_gift.cost: After the scene, the user marks +1 Obligation to the Inquisitor Prime.

rites.name: Rite of the Pure Flame
rites.materials: Ash from a burned grimoire or sigil-scarred candle.
rites.effect: Gain +2 dice to resist supernatural influence (fear, charm, possession) and +1 Armor vs. magical attacks. Undead/demonic foes suffer –1 die against you.
rites.push_it: Extend the effect to allies in Near range, but supernatural entities sense you immediately; mark 1 SB (Diamonds). Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Unclouded Eye
rites.materials: Silver dust stirred into holy water.
rites.effect: +2 dice to Investigate/Insight when spotting illusions, glamours, or magical deception. Cannot be surprised by sorcery this scene.
rites.push_it: For one exchange, pierce all illusions; mark 1 SB (Hearts). Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Cleansing Light
rites.materials: A shard of blessed mirror and consecrated oil.
rites.effect: Target a magical effect (ward, curse, enchantment). Test DV = Tier. On Hit: Dispel. On Partial: Weaken. On Miss: The effect lashes back, generating 1 SB.
rites.push_it: Dispel absolutely and trace its caster; mark +1 Obligation and 1 SB (Spades). Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +2) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Consecrated Ground
rites.materials: Relics from three rival faiths, salt, crushed gemstones.
rites.effect: Consecrate an area. Supernatural entities must pass Spirit+Endurance (DV 4) to enter. Undead/demonic suffer –2 dice inside. The site gains the [WARD] tag.
rites.push_it: Permanently sanctify a larger area, but start a Magical Dead Zone [6] timer and mark +2 Obligation. Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +3) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

rites.name: Rite of the Final Admonition
rites.materials: Ash from a destroyed spellbook, martyr's water, and the target's true name.
rites.effect: Attempt to annihilate one supernatural foe. Target tests Spirit+Endurance (DV 5). On Fail: destroyed outright. On Success: suffer Harm 3 and –2 dice this scene. Once per target only.
rites.push_it: Absolute destruction leaves behind Sanctified Ground; mark 2 SB (Diamonds). Cost: Mark +1 Obligation (total +3) or Mark +1 Fatigue.

cantors.name: The Cantor's Song
cantors.description: A Cantor of the Inquisitor Prime does not sing melodies – they chant liturgies of excision, flat, rhythmic recitations that scrub the air of taint. Their voice is used to purify a space before a hunt, to drown out a heretic's dying curse, or to march troops into battle with a single, unified note. Inquisitorial Cantors are rarely loved, but they are feared – and their songs are remembered long after the pyre has cooled.

cult.name: The Cult of the Iron Chorus
cult.description: The Prime's cults are militant orders – the Chain-Lanterns of Thepyrgos, the Censer-Knights of Ecktoria, the Spirit-Shield Correctors of Aeler. They gather in fortified chapter houses, not temples. A ritual of the Iron Chorus involves each member testifying to a corruption they have purged, then striking an iron bell with a hammer. The bell's tone is harsh and final. Their creed is stamped into every seal: 'What is pure endures. What is not is fuel.' Outsiders are not welcome; they are suspects until proven clean.

witchcraft.name: The Rite of Purification
witchcraft.description: A witch who walks with the Inquisitor Prime is often an exorcist scribe, a censer-bearer, or an inquisitorial archivist – a nun, monk, or scholar of one of the great purifying orders. Their magic is the art of liturgical cleansing: copying purification rites into iron-bound codices, blending ash and myrrh into sealing wax that repels spirits, or maintaining the reliquaries that hold the bones of saints who died hunting heretics. Their tools are not forge-hammers but censers, seals, and scourges – instruments of penitence and judgment.
witchcraft.lore: The inquisitorial witch learns to wield faith as a weapon. They are not healers – they are surgeons of the soul, cutting out corruption with cold precision. Their path is one of absolute certainty, and they walk it without mercy.
witchcraft.quote: Mercy is weakness. Purity is survival.

censer.name: The Censer of the Unforgiving Flame
censer.description: A brass censer hung on three chains, each link etched with a clause of the Inquisitor's Creed. Once per session, the witch may swing the censer to fill a zone with thick, bitter smoke. For the scene, any supernatural creature within the smoke suffers –1 die to all rolls, and any magical effect passing through the smoke is treated as one Tier lower for resistance. The censer can also be used to 'cense' a threshold: sprinkling ash from the censer across a doorway applies the [WARD] tag against minor spirits and undead until the next dawn.

hedge_gifts.name: Rite of the Soot Line
hedge_gifts.description: Once per scene, the witch may draw a line of ash and salt across a threshold (a door, a bridge, a window) while reciting a single verse from the Inquisitor's Litany. Until the next dawn, that line functions as a [WARD] against minor spirits (Cap 1–2) and all undead of Cap 2 or lower. A creature attempting to cross must test Spirit+Endurance (DV 3) or be turned back for that exchange. The line glows faintly when a lie is spoken within Near range.

monastic_tradition.name: The Iron Hand
monastic_tradition.description: Monks of the Iron Hand are living weapons of purity—trained to root out corruption, resist the taint of the supernatural, and deliver judgment without hesitation. They are relentless, incorruptible, and utterly without mercy for the guilty.
monastic_tradition.prerequisites: Spirit 3+, Resolve 2+, Rite of the Pure Flame or Cantor of the Inquisitor Prime.
monastic_tradition.quote: What is pure endures. What is not is fuel.
monastic_tradition.debt_resistant_frame: The Iron Hand does not borrow—it confiscates. Monks of the Inquisitor Prime gain +1 die to resist any magical debt, geas, or contract that would compel them to tolerate corruption or spare the guilty. If they succeed, the creditor's demand burns away in the light of purity—the obligation is annulled.

basic.name: Hunter's Instinct
basic.effect: You gain +1 die to Investigation and Notice when tracking or detecting supernatural creatures. Once per scene, you may ask the GM one yes/no question about a creature's nature or weakness.

advanced.name: Cleansing Strike
advanced.effect: When you hit a supernatural creature with a melee attack, you may choose to deal +1 Harm and impose –1 die on their next action as the Prime's light sears them.

master.name: Absolute Judgment
master.effect: Once per session, name a supernatural foe as utterly corrupt. For that scene, gain +3 dice against them, and any critical hit against them deals +2 Harm and may banish them permanently.
master.cost: 2 Fatigue and +1 Obligation to the Inquisitor Prime

monastic_tradition.corruption_note: Monks follow the patron's general Corruption track; the monastic path does not add a second one. Where a tradition needs its own, it must differ from the general track in kind, not degree.

corruption.benefit: Hunter's Instinct: +1 die to Notice magical auras or traps.
corruption.cost: Black-and-White Thinking: Must label others 'pure' or 'corrupt'; –1 die when navigating moral nuance.

corruption.benefit: Sanctified Weapon: Once/scene, your weapon ignores 1 Armor/Resist from supernatural foes.
corruption.cost: Purity Zeal: Exposure to filth or corruption causes 1 Fatigue.

corruption.benefit: Cold Clarity: +2 dice to resist deception, illusion, or mental sway.
corruption.cost: Suspicion: –1 die to social rolls with anyone you suspect of 'impurity.'

corruption.benefit: Burning Truth: Once/session, compel one target to answer truthfully (Resolve DV 4).
corruption.cost: Compulsion: Cannot ignore supernatural activity; hesitation costs 1 SB (Clubs).

corruption.benefit: Sterile Aura: Once/session, emit a presence that suppresses supernatural abilities (–2 dice in Near).
corruption.cost: Purity Addiction: Suffer 1 Fatigue when in a supernatural area without taking action against it.

corruption.benefit: Absolute Judgment: Once/session, name a supernatural foe as utterly corrupt. For that scene, gain +3 dice against them.
corruption.cost: Monomania: When invoked, you tunnel on that target, suffering –2 dice to all else. Your eyes glow faintly with inner flame, and heretics recognize you on sight.

playstyle_notes.description: The Inquisitor's rites protect against supernatural influence and help hunt or bind its sources. Followers grow certain that their own categories distinguish the innocent from the corrupt. Test that certainty with evidence: a prohibited practice saving lives, an approved officer abusing power, or a hunt whose target has been misidentified. Their conviction should create decisions, not certify their accusations as true.

sample_adventure.title: The Heretic's Mask
sample_adventure.description: A village on the edge of the Mistlands has been harboring a fugitive witch who fled the Inquisition. The Inquisitor Prime has dispatched a Censer-Knight to bring her to justice. The party must decide: protect the witch, who claims she is innocent, or aid the Inquisitor in their hunt. The village's bell-line is failing, and the fog is rising. Whoever wins, the dead will not stay quiet for long.
sample_adventure.quote: The flame that reveals the truth also burns the hand that holds it. Choose carefully, for the Inquisitor does not forgive.

appears_in_religions.note: Iron masks, blessed coal, and jurisdiction that does not stop at a border.
Lanterns carried on chains as a reminder of restraint that has never once stopped them.
Investigates broken oaths and brings the suit, including against the faith's own officers.
Invoked with the Pale Shepherd by those who burn what the Consuming Flame has touched.
The Flame-Wardens' coastal cousins, who drown rather than burn and call it a mercy.

orders_are_masks: An Order is the shape this Patron takes inside a religion — the office through which it is approached, named and made respectable. The same Patron therefore appears in faiths that despise each other, and rarely at the same rank.

guises.name: The Unquenchable Fire
guises.note: A sealed censer is passed before a hunt, and its smoke is remembered as evidence that the company stood together. Officers cite the Everflame when presenting the campaign to a congregation. Their claim does not make every Flame priest a servant of the Prime. Some priests have publicly refused the censer after learning whom the knights intended to bind.

guises.among: Aeler Iron Avengers and Spirit-Shield Correctors
guises.name: The Light of Forges
guises.note: A faceless iron figure stands among brands used to mark controlled workings. Its admirers point to incursions their predecessors contained and lives actually saved. The dispute begins when control of a dangerous working is extended into authority over every person whose craft differs from the approved one. Severe Himadri observance and the Prime's domination are not the same condition.

guises.name: The Gilded Judge
guises.note: The figure is dressed like an immaculate arbiter, with its face concealed by reflected light. Templars may understand their own violence as fidelity rather than anger. They can courteously receive a herald while refusing to hear the accused person's defense. The ceremony is sincerely believed and can sincerely authorize cruelty.

guises.name: The Keeper of the Approved Flame
guises.note: A bound lantern is carried into a room before an arcane demonstration. Scholars have accepted the protection and then discovered that the lantern's keeper claims the right to decide which demonstrations may ever occur. Some laboratories retain the protection while contesting the office. Others have become showrooms for powers whose captive bearers are never permitted to address the visitors.

provenance.origin: The Inquisitor Prime answers convictions of absolute purity and domination. The cult's militant orders preserve different accounts of the crises that justified their formation.
provenance.summary: Chapter memorials record real supernatural harms beside lists of successful hunts. The surviving community has reason to remember a company that stopped an incursion. Later chronicles sometimes extend that gratitude into authority over questions the original company never faced. A warrant granted for one danger becomes a precedent for identifying a much wider class of people as dangerous.
provenance.the_migration: Orders exchanged Cantors, restraint practices, and accounts of recognized signs. Ecktoria's Censer-Knights, Thepyrgos's Chain-Lanterns, and Aeler Correctors did not acquire identical interests through those exchanges. A scholar's demand to study a bound power, a commander's demand to deploy it, and a hold's fear of another breach could all be presented as purification. Their agreements often settled who would possess the captive without settling whose account of its nature was right.
provenance.why_it_took: Fear makes certainty attractive, especially after an event people could neither understand nor prevent. The Prime's rites can supply effective protection. Its servants then have a powerful argument for dismissing criticism: the protection worked. The leap from a real success to unlimited jurisdiction is where grateful households can find themselves submitting to an order they never thought they had invited to govern them.
provenance.note: A chapter's contradiction is visible in the bound powers it retains. What it calls intolerable in a neighbor may be called necessary when secured behind its own doors. Devotees defend the distinction as the victory of order over corruption. Critics need not deny the original danger to question who is being required to live in chains, or what the chapter now gains from keeping them there.

philosophy.name: Certainty That Feeds on Its Exceptions
philosophy.summary: The Prime teaches its servants to recognize their approved categories as reality. Disagreement then appears to confirm the need for stronger control.
philosophy.the_point: Effective protection can coexist with unjust accusation. A devotee who has saved lives may find it especially hard to admit that the next target has been chosen wrongly; the admission seems to threaten every earlier sacrifice as well.
philosophy.the_third_thing: A chapter can expose a corrupt officer without surrendering its doctrine. A more difficult reckoning concerns a faithful officer who applied the doctrine exactly. That is the case most likely to be closed before all its witnesses arrive.
philosophy.at_the_table: A bound supernatural being has genuinely attacked people in the past and is now forced to maintain a district's protection. The order calls release unthinkable; nearby households fear losing the ward. Give the party evidence about the being, the present restraint, and alternative protection. Do not make its former danger certify enslavement or require every accusation to be false for resistance to matter.
